feedback: If the child stops at a bare '5': ask 'five what? what is that for Sam?' — the calculation is right, only the interpretation needs prompting.
If the child endorses 35: 'you gave 20p and want 35p back — can you get more money by spending some?' Let them catch and reject the impossibility, then state the real change as '5p change'.
Direct feedback at the interpretation and the sense-check, not only at whether the arithmetic was correct.
activities.intendedInsight: A calculation is not finished when the number appears; it is finished when the number is read back into the story and checked for whether it could possibly be true. You cannot end up with MORE money after spending some.
learnerActions: Read a shop story, e.g. 'Sam has 20p in his purse and buys a sticker costing 15p. How much change does he get?'
Build a bar model of the situation: 20 as the whole, split into a 15 part and a mystery (change) part; or write a matching number sentence.
Work out the missing part to land on 5.
Complete a mandatory 'what does your 5 mean?' step: attach the unit and quantity, finishing the sentence '5p change'.
Pass a reasonableness check before the answer is accepted: decide whether a candidate answer could possibly be true in the story (e.g. flag that change greater than the amount paid is impossible).
activities.title: Model a shop story, then make the return trip

feedback: If the child adds the two numbers because a keyword suggested it, pause before any operation and model the situation on the bar first (e.g. 20 as the whole, 15 as a part).
Check that each number on the bar carries a unit and matches a real quantity in the story.
Ask 'what does this number mean here?' at the end, not just 'what's the answer?'
activities.intendedInsight: Bar models expose the structure of a situation — including part-whole and comparison relationships — so the child models the relationships rather than grabbing numbers and applying a keyword operation.
learnerActions: Draw a part-whole bar model for a word problem, labelling which part is the known quantity, which is the whole, and which is the unknown.
Use a comparison bar model to show two quantities side by side for a comparison problem (e.g. one ribbon longer than another).
Use a number line to represent money or measurement jumps when that fits the story better.
Attach units to each quantity on the model and to the final answer.
activities.title: Bar models for part-whole and comparison problems
